metadata.title: A radio signal, traced to a planet
metadata.author: Visual Journalism Desk
metadata.description: Astronomers using MeerKAT have localized auroral radio emission to the exoplanet Beta Pictoris b, not its star, and inferred a magnetic field of at least 1,250 gauss. The video explains the evidence, the measurement and its limits, how coverage framed it, and what remains unconfirmed. The study is a preprint that has not been peer reviewed.

accessibility.description: A tabletop explainer. A printed telescope image of the planet Beta Pictoris b; paper schematics of the star and planet; quote cards; a paper tuning dial that converts radio frequency into magnetic field strength; a bar chart comparing Earth, Jupiter and Beta Pictoris b; a timeline of earlier radio claims; and a closing sources sheet.

cue.text: For the first time, astronomers have pinned a radio
signal on a planet beyond our solar system.
Not on its star. On the planet itself.
The planet is Beta Pictoris b, a young
gas giant about 64 light-years away.
Co-author Yvette Cendes expects the first reaction: “When people
see ‘radio signal from an exoplanet,’ they think aliens.”
The team’s explanation is an aurora: the planet’s
own northern lights, shining in radio waves.
The work is a preprint, posted on September
15. It has not yet been peer reviewed.
The team, from the Harvard–Smithsonian Center for
Astrophysics and the University of Oregon, used
MeerKAT, a 64-dish radio array in South Africa.
Across four sessions, from February 2025 to May 2026, they
recorded bursts that repeated, plus a steady glow.
The bursts were 40 to 70 percent circularly polarized,
the signature expected from auroral radio emission.
The hard part was position. Seen from Earth, the planet
sits at most half an arcsecond from its star.
So the team tied their radio map to nine distant
quasars charted by the Gaia mission.
The signal lands on the planet’s expected position, and misses
the star by 4.4 sigma: odds of about six in a million.
They also tested the other suspects: the star,
its dust disk, its wind, a possible moon.
None of them produces a signal this strong.
The signal also measures the planet. In auroral emission, frequency
tracks magnetic field: 2.8 gigahertz per thousand gauss.
The emission reached 3.5 gigahertz. That
requires a field of at least 1,250 gauss.
Earth’s field is about half a gauss. Jupiter’s is about four.
The authors call it the first direct measurement
of an exoplanet’s magnetic field.
One caution: 3.5 gigahertz is also the
top of the receiver band MeerKAT used.
So 1,250 gauss is a floor. The true peak could
be higher than the telescope can hear.
A field that strong fits what dynamo models
predict for a young, massive giant planet.
Headlines called this a first in history.
That claim needs one qualifier.
In 2021, a LOFAR team reported a tentative signal from Tau
Boötis. Follow-up observations did not see it again.
In 2023, radio bursts from the star YZ
Ceti were tied, tentatively, to its
planet. The radio came from the star.
In 2024, this same team surveyed 140 exoplanets with the Very
Large Array and found no emission clearly from a planet.
What is new is the address: radio emission
placed on a planet, not on its star.
Coverage also rounded differently: 63 or
64 light-years, 10 or 12 Jupiter masses.
The number to keep is the paper’s:
at least 1,250 gauss.
Some stories tied the result to habitable worlds. Oxford astrophysicist
Suzanne Aigrain told Live Science: “A planet’s magnetic field shields
its atmosphere from the ‘wind’ of charged particles from its star.”
But Beta Pictoris b is a gas giant. The payoff
is the method, not a habitable world.
Open questions remain. Radio astronomer Joe Callingham,
who was not part of the study, told Science News:
“So TBD, but, compelling. It’s probably auroral.”
Two bursts about eight hours apart are comparable to
the planet’s eight-to-nine-hour day. A signal that
pulses with every turn has not yet been confirmed.
The team names seven more giant planets, in
five nearby systems, for the same method.
That needs telescopes five to seven times more sensitive,
the authors say: next-generation arrays such as
the Square Kilometre Array, now under construction.
For now, one planet beyond the solar system has
a measured magnetic field, pending peer review.
